title: CDC Confirms Third Measles Death of 2026 as U.S. Cases Top 4,400 in Worst Outbreak in Decades
excerpt: The CDC confirmed a third measles-related death in the United States this year, with 4,410 confirmed cases nationwide as of Oct. 15 — the country's worst measles outbreak in decades.
content:
The United States has recorded its third measles-related death of 2026, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed on Tuesday, as the country battles its worst measles outbreak in decades, according to Reuters.

The agency reported 4,410 confirmed cases nationwide as of Oct. 15, according to Reuters — far beyond the 2,289 cases recorded in all of 2025. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services told Reuters that the National Center for Health Statistics received a report of a measles-related death and verified that the disease was the underlying cause. The CDC did not name the states where the deaths occurred.

Pennsylvania has been hit hardest by the resurgence, logging 1,286 cases, according to Reuters. State health authorities there have reported five confirmed measles-associated deaths — all in unvaccinated individuals — as of Oct. 19, and officials are reviewing an additional death reported by the Franklin County coroner. The gap between the federal and state tolls follows the CDC’s switch to National Center for Health Statistics mortality data to track measles deaths, Reuters reported.

Last week, the CDC agreed to deploy additional support to Pennsylvania through its Epi-Aid emergency response program after the state formally requested federal help investigating the outbreak, according to Reuters.

“We should not have any measles deaths in the United States,” said William Moss, an epidemiology professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, noting the disease was declared eliminated in the country in 2000, according to Reuters. Federal data show the overwhelming majority of cases have occurred in people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. The CDC says the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is about 97 percent effective after two doses — a reminder worth heeding for South Texas families checking their children’s shot records.
